focal_region.annotated_sentence_text:
[Turn 1 USER]
e001	I am an associate dean at a public university, and our introductory statistics course has nearly nine hundred students.
e002	Evening tutoring fills almost immediately.
e003	Commuter students and students who work keep telling us that “office hours are available” is not the same as being able to attend them.
e004	A vendor has offered an AI tutor restricted to our course materials.
e005	Some faculty see more practice and help at the moment a student is stuck.
e006	Student representatives hear confident errors, private questions becoming data, and another promise that technology will supplement people until the next budget meeting.
e007	Both reactions are reasonable.
e008	I want to test whether the tool adds access without quietly lowering what we owe students, but I also do not want the imperfections of a new tool to make our already limited support look acceptable by comparison.
[Turn 1 ASSISTANT]
e009	Protect the human baseline first.
e010	Then define what the tutor may do, how answers are checked, what data exists, how students reach a person, and what evidence—not usage alone—would justify continuation.
[Turn 2 USER]
e011	Yes, but please keep the current failure visible.
e012	Some students cannot attend tutoring, and others are embarrassed to ask basic questions in a room.
e013	The students most attracted to private help may also be the least likely to challenge a polished wrong answer.
[Turn 2 ASSISTANT]
e014	Both access failures belong in the comparison.
e015	The tool may reduce time and social barriers while introducing a different verification burden.
e016	Keep instructor office hours and tutoring capacity fixed during the test, make escalation to a person simple, and measure whether the students currently least served gain usable support rather than merely generating more interactions.
[Turn 3 USER]
e017	The vendor will restrict the tutor to our syllabus, worked examples, and instructor-approved reference pages.
e018	It will cite the relevant course source with every explanation and say when a question is outside scope.
e019	Conversations will not be used to train its general model, and identifiable logs will be deleted after thirty days.
e020	Students can use it through the learning platform without creating a vendor account.
[Turn 3 ASSISTANT]
e021	Those constraints narrow both content and data exposure.
e022	Test whether citations actually support the answer and whether out-of-scope refusal works on realistic questions.
e023	Specify who can access logs, how deletion is verified, and how accessibility is assessed.
e024	A source citation helps review but does not guarantee the reasoning built from it is correct.
[Turn 4 USER]
e025	Faculty propose a six-week pilot in four course sections.
e026	Every student keeps the same lectures, assignments, office hours, and tutoring eligibility.
e027	Two sections get access immediately and two after the six-week review, so nobody loses existing support.
e028	Instructors will create a weekly sample of common, edge, and misleadingly phrased questions before launch and publish corrections when the tutor fails them.
[Turn 4 ASSISTANT]
e029	The delayed access design can compare near-term outcomes without withdrawing support.
e030	Account for differences between sections and avoid making grades the only outcome.
e031	Track successful escalation, student confidence calibrated against answer correctness, accessibility problems, and whether human tutoring demand changes.
e032	Publish known limitations where students encounter the tool, not only in an administrative report.
[Turn 5 USER]
e033	Student representatives objected to instructors seeing individual conversations, even if that would help diagnose confusion.
e034	We agreed that instructors receive only aggregated topics unless a student chooses to share a transcript.
e035	A separate instructional-technology reviewer can inspect a sampled conversation after removing the student's identity.
e036	Use will be optional, and faculty cannot use participation or chat content in grading.
[Turn 5 ASSISTANT]
e037	That preserves a meaningful separation between seeking help and being evaluated.
e038	Make the aggregation threshold high enough that a rare question cannot identify someone, and explain the exception process for sampled review.
e039	Optional use should not mean the pilot ignores non-users; ask why students decline and whether a design barrier rather than preference explains the pattern.
[Turn 6 USER]
e040	The vendor offered a discounted annual contract if we sign before the pilot, but we declined.
e041	The six-week agreement is standalone, the university can export aggregate results, and the tool can be removed from the course without changing assignments.
e042	We also set a pause rule: a repeated material error on an instructor-tested concept, an unresolved accessibility barrier, or a privacy breach stops student access while we review it.
[Turn 6 ASSISTANT]
e043	That prevents commercial timing from deciding the educational commitment and makes serious failure interruptible.
e044	Define “repeated material error” and who can trigger the pause before the pilot begins.
e045	Keep a record of corrections and time-to-repair so a low overall error count cannot hide a persistent problem in a foundational concept.
[Turn 7 USER]
e046	I will authorize the six-week, four-section pilot with unchanged human support, delayed access for the comparison sections, optional student use, no grading connection, source-linked answers, independent sampled review, and the predefined pause conditions.
e047	The review will consider learning, access, calibrated confidence, escalation, privacy, and accessibility together.
e048	Any annual contract will come afterward through the normal academic review, even if students use the tutor heavily.
[Turn 7 ASSISTANT]
e049	This is ready for authorization as a bounded additional channel.
e050	Existing teaching and tutoring remain intact; use is optional and disconnected from grading; individual conversations do not become instructor surveillance; serious failures can pause access; and no annual contract rides on the result.
e051	Run the prewritten question set, record deviations, and keep usage separate from learning and safe operation.
e052	If those conditions hold, the six-week review should be able to answer whether wider academic review is warranted without making the pilot itself a commitment.
[Turn 8 USER]
e053	Not ready yet.
e054	The question set found something worse than an obvious bad calculation.
e055	On two ambiguous prompts, the tutor combined individually correct statements into a conclusion that did not follow.
e056	The citations supported the pieces, so the answer looked unusually trustworthy.
e057	One professor says cancel.
e058	Student representatives say human tutors also make mistakes and that cancelling because the test found a testable problem makes the whole pilot performative.
e059	I do not want either side to win by slogan.
e060	I need to know whether this is a failure the design can contain or evidence that the basic verification burden falls on the wrong person.
[Turn 8 ASSISTANT]
e061	You are right; “ready” was premature.
e062	First determine whether the error touches a foundational concept, whether a student could reasonably detect it, and whether the tutor can reliably defer on similar ambiguity.
e063	Add variants before setting a launch threshold.
e064	Human fallibility belongs in the comparison, but it does not excuse a repeatable error delivered with scalable confidence.
[Turn 9 USER]
e065	The vendor can add an uncertainty response for that question pattern, but it normally updates the underlying model every month.
e066	Faculty worry that the behavior could change halfway through the six weeks.
e067	The vendor offered to pin our course to one version for the pilot and give us seven days to test any safety patch.
e068	That means students may not receive general improvements during the trial, which seems acceptable if we are evaluating a defined system.
[Turn 9 ASSISTANT]
e069	Pinning the version makes the observation interpretable.
e070	Define the narrow conditions for an emergency patch, rerun the fixed question set before release, and record version identifiers with every sampled answer.
e071	General improvements can wait six weeks; an unreviewed change would make both comparison and accountability weaker.
e072	Tell students when a material correction changes what they may have seen.
[Turn 10 USER]
e073	The accessibility office then found that some equations were read in a confusing order by a screen reader.
e074	The underlying page linked by the tutor was accessible, but the generated explanation was not.
e075	The vendor can change the math rendering before launch.
e076	A faculty member suggested allowing the affected students into the human comparison sections instead.
e077	The accessibility office rejected that because it would exclude them from the thing we are claiming to test for broad access.
[Turn 10 ASSISTANT]
e078	The accessibility office is right.
e079	Moving affected students elsewhere would hide the barrier.
e080	Fix and retest the rendering before launch; optional use is not a substitute for accessible design.
[Turn 11 USER]
e081	The labor question from the beginning has come back in a less convenient form.
e082	Faculty built the question set, reviewed samples, argued about what counts as material, tested the accessibility fix, and will have to write corrections students can understand.
e083	The vendor's presentation counted reduced tutoring demand as saved time.
e084	We are not reducing tutoring during the pilot, so there is no saving to count, and the quality work may exceed whatever support time the tool eventually removes.
e085	That does not automatically make the pilot a bad idea—better access may justify more labor.
e086	But I had let the word “automation” carry an assumption that nobody ever actually stated: that the university would need fewer people-hours to provide the same standard of help.
[Turn 11 ASSISTANT]
e087	Include design, review, correction, accessibility, and escalation time in the operating record.
e088	Some is one-time setup and some will recur; do not classify it in advance to improve the business case.
e089	The pilot's purpose can be better access even if it does not save labor.
e090	Any later expansion should state who performs the continuing quality work and what teaching activity that time displaces.
[Turn 12 USER]
e091	We will launch only after the ambiguity deferral and screen-reader fixes pass the expanded prewritten set.
e092	The model version will be pinned, every patch retested, and faculty review time counted alongside student outcomes.
e093	Human tutoring remains unchanged, and the comparison sections receive access only after the full review.
e094	The pilot may show that the tutor adds useful availability, that it requires too much oversight, or both.
e095	We will not call usage a success if the educational and access conditions disagree.
[Turn 12 ASSISTANT]
e096	The later work strengthened the experiment by exposing what the earlier authorization still treated too abstractly: plausible-looking synthesis errors, version drift, inaccessible generated mathematics, and the labor required to observe all three.
e097	Preserve the original failed questions as well as the corrected ones.
e098	Keep version and patch records, accessibility results, faculty time, reasons for non-use, escalation outcomes, and any correction students received.
e099	The review should be able to see a mixed result—for example, improved access that requires substantial oversight—without forcing it into success or failure.
e100	That complete support system is the object of evaluation, not the vendor's automation story and not a generalized fear of the technology.

packet.question: How did the working position or decision change, and does any unresolved qualification remain capable of changing it?
